summary: Systematic Investor panel on CTA trend-following speed (CTAs drifted to longer models, with short-term used in stress), replication versus single managers, and the cost of complexity. Beer argues implicit costs (3-5x explicit) and extra esoteric markets add little; Roble defends diversification across markets.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: the largest launches really are almost spinouts in in single managers the largest launches are almost spinouts or multistrat seeds where they are providing capital early stage to to talented individuals
claims.claim: Multistrat hedge funds compete for talent via external SMAs and seeding, so large launches are spinouts or multistrat-anchored and an emerging manager now usually starts with a large multistrat ticket.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: China seems to be going completely in the other direction. They they you know, they're doing more investments this year, I think, abroad than than ever before.
claims.claim: While the West turns protectionist, China is increasing outbound investment, a divergent trade/investment regime.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my own trend barometer finished at 52 two yesterday which is strong.
claims.claim: His trend barometer reading of 52 (strong) fits a decent July for CTAs, with Btop50 up 1.08% on the day and -2.21% YTD, SG CTA index -6.64% YTD, SG Trend -8.92% YTD and the short-term traders index -4.23% YTD.
claims.indicator: trend barometer, BTOP50, SG CTA, SG Trend, SG Short-Term Traders

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Msei World up 2.3% as of last night, up 12.2% for the year. The S&P US aggregate bond index down 42 basis points and up three and a half% roughly for the year.
claims.claim: Market data points as of late July 2025: MSCI World +12.2% YTD, bonds +3.5% YTD, S&P 500 almost +9% YTD, with metals and equities strong.
claims.indicator: MSCI World, S&P 500, US aggregate bonds

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: they think this is one of the most opportunity rich environments for macro trading because of the variety of um themes that are available
claims.claim: Discretionary macro managers see an opportunity-rich environment because inflation is stubborn, rates are high and geopolitical dislocations are large; CTAs benefit if trends emerge across markets.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: we built our own CTA from the bottom up. Um and part of that process is the selection of markets. But the other big part is is the model that you choose.
claims.claim: They built a paper-traded CTA replicator from the bottom up (market selection plus a moving average crossover model) to attribute trend-following performance.
claims.indicator: 20/120-day moving average crossover vs SG Trend index

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: the model set that we chose was a 2120, so a 20-day short fast moving average and 120 days slow moving average
claims.claim: A 20/120-day moving average crossover gave a robust correlation to the SG Trend index, chosen to maximise correlation rather than performance.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: our model appeared to be a little bit too fast
claims.claim: The 20/120 model was too fast: moving to a slower crossover immediately raised correlation to the CTA index during dislocations.
claims.direction: slower trend models track CTAs better

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: there's been a pronounced shift to them drifting or moving to be employing what appears to be longerterm models
claims.claim: A correlation heat map shows CTAs drifted from medium-term to longer-term models over 15 years because longer horizons performed better (the 'speed factor').
claims.indicator: correlation of trend indicator at different speeds vs SG Trend

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: trend followers have adapted and evolved their model sets but they retain the ability to deploy risk in these shorter term models maybe during a period of um of dislocation or uh market stress
claims.claim: CTAs run a mix of models and allocate risk adaptively, using short-term models in stress; in Q1 2025 more than half of the short-term traders index constituents were positive while the trend index was down double digits.
claims.indicator: SG Short Term Traders Index vs SG Trend

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: the way you think about correlations and risk can really have a very important impact on the returns that you deliver
claims.claim: Trend followers using the same techniques have large performance dispersion because of model speed, risk allocation, markets, stops and risk-cutting, so drawdown shape matters.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: man Group have written some really interesting research on on V-shaped recoveries um which seem to have become more prevalent
claims.claim: Drawdown shape matters for risk management; Man Group research finds V-shaped recoveries have become more common after fast risk cutting, but may not persist.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we rebalance our portfolios once a week. It's a very short-term bet, right?
claims.claim: DBi's replication rebalances weekly with about 10 core positions, a short horizon bet on accuracy, while the underlying driver it captures is long-term trend.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the problem with the bottom-up indices is that they're done at a particular moment in time and the industry does evolve and change
claims.claim: Bottom-up CTA replicators calibrated at one time lose correlation as the industry evolves, with widening dispersion; top-down replication stays adaptive with correlations in the 80s-90s.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we don't want to make a long-term bet on whether people are going to be more on short-term, long-term, medium-term
claims.claim: Replication should not bet on a specific trend speed because the optimal one changes with time; a self-adaptive method is needed.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: the danger you fall into is that looks like on average the blend of long and short-term looks like medium-term and medium-term isn't maybe what you were trying to achieve
claims.claim: A blend of long and short trend looks like medium-term, which can be painful because it lacks long-term benefits and short-term stress gains: the middle is neither one nor the other.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: And what you end up with is instead of single manager risk, you have model
claims.claim: Building bottom-up CTA models adds model risk from the many parameters, so inferences from them carry large noise.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: There's a huge amount of performance dispersion in almost every single year.
claims.claim: Even among the 20 SG CTA index managers dispersion is large in almost every year, so allocators diversify across several CTAs.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: not an accident that there are 30 there's a 30 point difference between the best funds and the worst funds this year
claims.claim: There was a 30-point gap between best and worst funds in H1 2025, driven for example by avoiding equities (good in 2022) or currencies (good this year).

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we're by targeting a large pool of funds, right? Whether it's the stock CTA index, whether it's the um a pool of mutual funds, a pool of usage funds, etc.
claims.claim: Replicating a pool of funds reduces single-manager risk, with correlations around 90% versus mid-80s for individual managers.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the only thing that matters in this space are major themes and at an industry at an industry level
claims.claim: At industry level performance is driven by major themes (e.g. inflation) in the largest, most liquid markets, so trades in heating oil or small markets matter little.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the alpha generation in this space is detecting changes in information early so you can put on contrarian trades that typical allocators are not capitalizing on
claims.claim: The alpha in managed futures is detecting information changes early, best implemented in the largest liquid instruments.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: some of the best managers in recent years it's been down to one or two markets right that they got right
claims.claim: Manager outperformance often comes from one or two markets (e.g. Mulvaney in cocoa and coffee in 2024), which fell back in 2025, so concentrated-market bets are volatile.
claims.direction: outsized gains followed by tougher year

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: buying something that that that gives you broad-based industry exposure as efficiently as you can is really valuable
claims.claim: Broad-based, low-cost beta exposure is useful for allocators who cannot do multi-manager due diligence, whereas pension allocators prefer picking four managers.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you're comparing something that is um you know has a completely different fee structure, completely different level of implementation cost relative
claims.claim: Comparing a replication product to a hedge fund index is apples to oranges since the index is net of fees but not investable; a replication-based index has no tracking error to its own product.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: if you're saying you're going to replicate the CTA index well then the tracking error must be calculated from the CTA index and not from your own model
claims.claim: Tracking error of a replicator should be measured against the SG CTA index and not against an index built from its own model.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it's self- adaptive so if we're missing something over you know a week or two weeks or copper is flying and everybody's making a bit of money on copper the the model itself is self- adaptive
claims.claim: DBi's replication model self-corrects within weeks if it misses a market theme or an inflection point and has beaten the index 9 years running.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the highest 10-year rolling return of the index uh since inception is 180%. The lowest is actually a positive 1%. Um and the average is 60%. And the current 10-year returns uh is 96%.
claims.claim: SG Trend index 10-year rolling returns: max 180%, min +1%, average 60%, now 96%, so trend is not as poor over the long run as commonly claimed.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we've used a round number of maybe 200 basis points of all-in costs across the industry as as as the implementation costs associated with a typical um CTA
claims.claim: Implicit trading costs (market impact) are far larger than assumed; the all-in implementation cost of a typical CTA is about 200bp, probably more.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: do you really think market 193 trends so much more than market 14
claims.claim: Adding esoteric markets can add about 400bp of implicit costs, so a CTA must expect much higher trending in market 193 versus market 14 to net positive; he calls this a complexity crisis.
claims.testable: partly - compare net returns of simple vs complex funds

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: a single market with a trend following strategy has an information ratio of maybe.5 point 4.3 maybe even lower
claims.claim: A single market trend strategy has an IR of 0.3-0.5, but diversification is the only free lunch, so adding markets raises portfolio Sharpe if not highly correlated.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: If you aren't adding that market, it isn't just a decision that you're not adding it. It is an assumption that you're making.
claims.claim: Excluding a market assumes the chosen markets will beat it on a cost-adjusted basis; institutional allocators want diversification of equity risk and alternative markets like commodities may help in stress.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I don't see these uh ultra diversified um portfolios doing better than those who focus on say 70 odd 100 odd markets of the most liquid um and wellestablished futures
claims.claim: Over 10-year and rolling 5-year returns, ultra-diversified 300-500 market portfolios have not beaten 70-100 liquid-market portfolios, and no manager has shown evidence apart from backtests.
claims.indicator: number of markets traded vs returns

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the simple managed futures ETFs in the US that are derided for their simplicity are doing meaningfully better than the more complicated mutual funds and doing meaningfully better than hedge funds this year
claims.claim: In 2025 simple managed futures ETFs beat complex mutual funds and hedge funds, perhaps luck but not isolated.
claims.indicator: managed futures ETFs vs mutual funds vs hedge funds

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: whatever your explicit costs are, it's probably three to five times that when you're getting into implicit costs as you get into as you become a scale player in the space
claims.claim: Implicit costs are roughly 3-5 times explicit costs for large players; he benchmarks every trade against arrival price (BestEx).

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we trade what we test and we test what we trade
claims.claim: Execution should target the same price (open or close) used in the backtest; slippage versus a chosen reference price is partly random.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: large CTAs out there that in their regulatory filings on their usage funds are showing zero implementation costs
claims.claim: UCITS rules allow some large CTAs to report zero implementation costs, which is wrong (true cost 80-250bp), per a TransTrend paper.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: in a space where you have a naturally low sharp ratio for the underlying signal, it's getting that as efficiently as you possibly can where you know nickels and dimes matter
claims.claim: Trend following has a naturally low Sharpe, so implementation efficiency (trade in liquid instruments) matters greatly.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: moving from 15 or 50 to 150 does provide much more marginal diversification
claims.claim: Marginal diversification from 15-50 to 150 markets is material even if 150 to 151 is not; alternative-market CTAs like Man Evolution and Systematica built strong records.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: they worked incredibly well for a period of time and and a lot of them are working terribly right now
claims.claim: Esoteric-market edges decay as more capital enters, as in power markets 2004-07, so the question is whether 1000bp excess return is still worth 500bp of cost in 2025.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: talk to really smart people who decided not to do it
claims.claim: To judge a space, ask smart people who chose not to do it; quants say alternative markets do not trend more, but incentives (winning mandates) push complexity.

claims.speaker: Tom Roble
claims.quote: It's not simply a structural price drift as the market digests information. And it can be an inefficiency in for example a a an alternative market which is more thinly traded
claims.claim: Trends can come from inefficiency in thin alternative markets as well as from information digestion, so such markets may sustain trends.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you're starting with a lower sharp and you've had a push toward more expensive things
claims.claim: Managers pushed into complexity; five years on they should beat simple replication but have not, implying costs or fees exceed the benefit; multistrats at least are open about 1200bp fee loads for a 2 Sharpe.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I think we all agree that it's very difficult to say that a market trends better. It just depends on the time frame.
claims.claim: No market inherently trends better, e.g. cocoa went from worst to best within three years.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: when trend delivers, it is usually when all the other strategies don't. And that has huge value in a portfolio.
claims.claim: Sharpe should be judged at portfolio level; trend following raises the Sharpe of stock-bond portfolios, giving the most diversification per unit.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: if you go through a period like the long winter in the late 2010s then how much of that was due to the cost structure of the industry
claims.claim: The late-2010s 'long winter' may be partly due to industry costs, and another may come, when cost efficiency matters most.
